quests.instruction: What is a home?
quests.correctAnswer: A place to live and rest 🏠
options: A place to shop for food 🛒
A place to live and rest 🏠
quests.hint: Which of these is somewhere you come back to every day, instead of just visiting?
quests.explanation: A home is where people live, rest, and keep the things that matter to them. Shops and libraries are places we visit.
quests.funFact: Homes can be as different as a big house on a hill or a small flat in a tall building. What they share is that someone lives there.

quests.instruction: Some families live in a house of their own. Others live in a building where lots of homes sit side by side and on top of each other. What is that kind of building called?
quests.hint: Only one of these has families sleeping and cooking behind its separate doors.
quests.explanation: In an apartment building, every family has its own home inside one big building. Houses and apartments both count as homes.
quests.funFact: Some apartment buildings are so tall that people ride an elevator to reach their front door.

quests.instruction: Which job does a home do for the people who live in it?
quests.hint: Consider what happens to you in a storm when you are inside a building compared with standing outside.
quests.explanation: Walls and a roof keep out rain, wind, heat, and cold, so a home is a safe, comfortable place to rest.
quests.funFact: Long before cities existed, people were already building shelters out of stone, wood, and animal skins.

quests.instruction: A heavy shower is falling. Which part of a house sits on top and stops the rain from getting in?
quests.hint: It is the highest part of the building, above the ceiling and above everyone's head.
quests.explanation: The roof covers the building so rain and snow stay out. Walls stand at the sides, and floors are underneath you.
quests.funFact: Where snow is heavy, roofs are often built steep so the snow slides off. In hot, dry places many roofs are flat.

quests.instruction: Bare feet, fuzzy socks, a rolled-out rug: they all rest on the same part of a room. Which part?
quests.hint: Your socks touch it all day, but your head never does.
quests.explanation: The floor is the flat surface you walk, sit, and play on. The ceiling is the opposite: the surface overhead.
quests.funFact: Floors can be wood, tile, stone, or concrete. People choose what suits the room and the climate.

quests.instruction: Which part of a house lets daylight in and lets you look outside, even when it is shut?
quests.hint: One of these is made so that light can pass right through it.
quests.explanation: Windows are made of clear glass, so light comes in and you can see out. Many can open for fresh air too. A door is mainly for walking through.
quests.funFact: Before glass was common, many windows were just openings covered with cloth, paper, or wooden shutters.

quests.instruction: You hear water running and see a toothbrush sitting by the sink. Which room are you most likely in?
quests.hint: Check what is next to the sink: pots and plates, or something for your teeth?
quests.explanation: Bathrooms are where people wash up and look after their bodies. Kitchens have sinks too, but those are for dishes and food.
quests.funFact: Different places use different words for this room: bathroom, washroom, or even loo.

quests.instruction: A delicious smell drifts through the home: something is baking. Which room is it coming from?
quests.hint: Follow your nose to the place where meals are made.
quests.explanation: Food is prepared and cooked in the kitchen, so cooking smells usually start there.
quests.funFact: Many kitchens have a fan or a window to carry steam and cooking smells outside.

quests.instruction: Pillows, a soft blanket, and a small night lamp are all waiting. Which space were they set up for?
quests.hint: Those things are for resting your body, not for eating or washing clothes.
quests.explanation: Pillows, blankets, and a lamp make a bedroom comfortable for sleeping.
quests.funFact: Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night.

quests.instruction: On Friday night the whole family piles together to watch a movie. Where in the home are they most likely to gather?
quests.hint: Look for the space with comfy seats meant for everyone, not just one person.
quests.explanation: The living room is a shared space for relaxing and spending time together. Some homes call it a lounge or a family room.
quests.funFact: In some homes the living area and kitchen are one open space, so people can chat while someone cooks.

quests.instruction: Plates are set out, chairs are pulled in, and everyone sits down for dinner. What is this part of the home called?
quests.hint: It is not where the food is cooked, but where it is eaten.
quests.explanation: People eat together in the dining area. In some homes it is a separate room; in others it is just a table near the kitchen.
quests.funFact: Not every family eats at a table. In many places people sit on mats or cushions around a low table or a cloth on the floor.

quests.instruction: You walk through the front door and want to take off your shoes and hang up your coat. Which space is made for that?
quests.hint: It is the first space you step into after coming inside.
quests.explanation: An entry area, sometimes called a foyer or an entryway, gives shoes and coats a spot near the door so dirt stays out of the rooms.
quests.funFact: In many countries people take their shoes off at the door to keep floors clean.

quests.instruction: Some homes have an open space outside where plants grow and kids can play. Which of these is it?
quests.hint: The other two are tucked away indoors, above or below the rooms. Which one has sky overhead?
quests.explanation: A garden or yard is open to the sky. Attics and basements are closed-in spaces inside the building.
quests.funFact: Gardens come in all sizes, from fields behind a farmhouse to a tiny strip of soil beside a front door.

quests.instruction: Which of these is NOT usually found inside a home?
quests.hint: Two of these have your own roof and walls. One is a spot out on the street.
quests.explanation: Bedrooms and bathrooms are rooms inside a home. A bus stop is a public place outside that everyone shares.
quests.funFact: Roads, parks, and bus stops are shared by a whole neighborhood, while the rooms of a home belong to the people who live there.

quests.instruction: Aisha's flat is on the third floor and has no yard. Where can she step outside for fresh air without leaving her home?
quests.hint: Look for a small platform that sticks out from an upper floor.
quests.explanation: A balcony gives people in apartments a small outdoor space attached to their home, high above the ground.
quests.funFact: Many people grow herbs and flowers in pots on balconies, turning a tiny space into a mini garden.

quests.instruction: Mr. Lee lives in the next building and waves hello every morning. What do we call him?
quests.hint: Think about distance: he is close to your home, but he does not live inside it.
quests.explanation: A neighbor is someone who lives near you. A guest visits your home for a while, and family members often live with you.
quests.funFact: In many communities neighbors share tools, borrow ingredients, and look out for each other.

quests.instruction: Numbers, a street name, and a city: together they tell people exactly where a home is. What is this called?
quests.hint: Delivery drivers look for it on a parcel before they start driving.
quests.explanation: An address names the exact location of a home in words and numbers, so mail, deliveries, and visitors can find the right place.
quests.funFact: On many streets, house numbers go up one side with odd numbers and the other side has even numbers.

quests.instruction: A delivery driver stands outside your door and wants you to know they have arrived. What can they press?
quests.hint: Pressing it makes a sound inside, so the people at home know someone is outside.
quests.explanation: A doorbell tells people inside that a visitor is at the door. Always ask a grown-up before opening the door to someone.
quests.funFact: Some doorbells have a tiny camera, so families can see who is outside before they answer.

quests.instruction: Mia is comparing three homes. Which one probably has the most rooms?
quests.hint: More space usually means more walls dividing it into separate rooms.
quests.explanation: Bigger homes usually have space for more separate rooms. Studios and tiny cabins fit everything into just a few.
quests.funFact: Some homes have only one big room, while others have a dozen or more.

quests.instruction: Dev's family lives in a studio flat with no separate bedroom. Where is his bed?
quests.hint: A studio fits several jobs into one space.
quests.explanation: In a studio, one main room is used for sleeping, sitting, and often eating. One room can do more than one job.
quests.funFact: People in small homes often pick furniture that does two jobs, like a sofa that turns into a bed.

quests.instruction: Which of these might a home NOT have and still be a perfectly good home?
quests.hint: Think about homes in the middle of a busy city.
quests.explanation: Plenty of homes come with a garage and plenty do not. A home mainly needs shelter: a roof, walls, and a place to rest.
quests.funFact: In crowded cities many families park in shared lots or on the street because their buildings have no garage.

quests.instruction: Which of these buildings is NOT somewhere people usually live?
quests.hint: People go there during the day to learn, then head back to their homes.
quests.explanation: A school is for learning. People spend part of the day there and then go home. Cottages and townhouses are homes.
quests.funFact: The word 'home' can also mean the town or country where you feel you belong.

quests.instruction: You open a door and spot a sofa, a rug, and a shelf of family photos. Where are you most likely standing?
quests.hint: Notice the family photos: they belong to people who live there.
quests.explanation: Sofas, rugs, and family photos are signs that people live in a place and have made it their own.
quests.funFact: Furniture stores arrange sofas and shelves into little model rooms to show how a home might look.

quests.instruction: Which of these places is shared by the whole neighborhood, not just one family?
quests.hint: Look for the one you could not walk into and call your own.
quests.explanation: A playground is a public place for everyone. A bedroom and a kitchen belong to the home where a family lives.
quests.funFact: Neighborhood parks and playgrounds are often looked after by a town or city so everyone can use them.

quests.instruction: Which daily need does a bathroom help people meet?
quests.hint: A sink, a shower, and soap all point to the same need.
quests.explanation: Washing hands, bathing, and brushing teeth keep your body clean and healthy. That is the bathroom's job.
quests.funFact: Washing hands with soap for about 20 seconds helps wash away most germs.

quests.instruction: At dinnertime a family wants to eat together. Which piece of furniture gives them a surface for their plates?
quests.hint: It needs a flat top at the right height for plates and elbows.
quests.explanation: A table gives everyone a flat surface to share a meal. Bookshelves and coat racks are for storing things.
quests.funFact: In some homes the same table is used for homework, crafts, and dinner.

quests.instruction: The sun has gone down and the room is dark. What do people switch on so they can see?
quests.hint: Only one of these makes brightness of its own.
quests.explanation: Lights let us see and move around safely after dark. A fan moves air, and a mirror only reflects light that is already there.
quests.funFact: Before electric lights, many homes were lit with candles and oil lamps.

quests.instruction: Two of these are parts of a house. Which one is NOT?
quests.hint: The other two stay put once the house is built. This one can roll away.
quests.explanation: Roofs and floors are parts of the building itself. A bicycle is a belonging that you keep at or near a home.
quests.funFact: Builders usually start with the foundation, then the floors and walls, and finish with the roof.

quests.instruction: Lina's home has two floors. Omar's home is a one-floor flat. What is true about their homes?
quests.hint: Does a home have to be a certain size or shape to count?
quests.explanation: Homes can be tall or flat, big or small, in a city or in the countryside. A place is a home when people live and feel safe there.
quests.funFact: People live in houseboats and in homes built into hillsides, shaping their homes to fit where they live.

quests.instruction: Zara comes in from the garden, goes through the front door, and walks to her bedroom. Which of these does she reach LAST?
quests.hint: Put the places in order, like steps on a path: outside, entrance, then inside.
quests.explanation: She goes from the garden to the front door and then through the home to her bedroom. Retelling a walk in order helps you picture how a home is laid out.
quests.funFact: In many homes, shared areas sit near the entrance and bedrooms are farther in, for privacy.
